usage: 쓰다 is the plain everyday verb coworkers use
작성하다 is the formal register for emails and notices
제출하다 is for officially handing it in
검토하다 is what a superior does to your draft
examples: 이건 무슨 보고서예요?
What report is this?
simple: 무슨 + noun asks 'what kind of'
오늘까지 보고서를 제출해야 해요.
I have to submit the report by today.
everyday: 까지 marks the deadline 'by'
팀장님이 보고서를 다시 쓰래요. 주말에도 야근이에요.
The team lead told me to rewrite the report. I'm working late even on the weekend.
real situation: 쓰래요 is contracted 쓰라고 해요, reported command
nuance: 보고서 is the standard word for any written work document, from a quick 주간 보고서 (weekly report) to a thick 출장 보고서 (trip report). It is Sino-Korean: 報告書, literally 'report-tell-document', where the 書 ending signals a formal written paper (compare 계획서 plan, 신청서 application form). The dividing line learners must feel is 보고서 (the paper you hand in) vs 발표 (the spoken presentation you give from it) vs 보고 (the act of reporting up): you 보고서를 작성해서 그걸로 발표해요. Register-wise 작성하다 belongs in formal/email speech while plain 쓰다 is fine between coworkers. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') because English says 'make a report' — in Korean 보고서를 만들다 sounds like physically constructing an object; a document is 쓰다 or 작성하다.

Confusing 보고서 (the written document) with 발표 (the spoken presentation) — you write a 보고서 and then give a 발표 about it
Writing 보고서 하다; the noun has no 하다 verb, so use 보고서를 쓰다 or, for the act of reporting, the separate verb 보고하다

usage: the default way to ask the due date
지키다 literally 'protect/keep', the set partner verb
다가오다 paints it as nearing you
to be chased by a deadline
쫓기다 'be chased', the idiom for crunch
examples: 마감이 언제예요?
When's the deadline?
simple: 언제 'when' + 예요
이번엔 꼭 마감을 지킬게요.
This time I'll definitely meet the deadline.
everyday: ㄹ게요 is a personal promise to the listener
마감에 쫓겨서 점심도 못 먹었어요.
Chased by the deadline, I couldn't even eat lunch.
real situation: 도 'even' + 못 'couldn't' stacks the hardship
nuance: 마감 is a native Korean noun (from the verb 막다 'to block/close off') meaning the point at which something is sealed shut: a report's due date, an application cutoff, a shop's last order, even a magazine going to press. The near-synonym confusion is with 기한 and 데드라인: 기한 (期限) is the dry, official 'time limit/term' you see on documents (제출 기한), while 마감 feels more like the live moment things close, and 데드라인 is a borrowed buzzword. Its signature collocation is the idiom 마감에 쫓기다 (chased by the deadline), the universal way to describe last-minute panic. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'meet a deadline' onto 만나다 ('meet a person'): you do NOT 마감을 만나다 — you 마감을 지키다 (keep/protect it). Note 지키다 is the same verb used for keeping a promise (약속을 지키다), which is the right mental image.

usage: 받다 'receive' — you, the junior, receive it
올리다 'send up', because it goes up the ladder
나다 'be issued', intransitive, it happens to you
who signs and in what order
examples: 이거 결재 받았어요?
Did this get approved?
simple: dropped 를 in casual speech, rising intonation = question
방금 결재 올렸으니까 확인 부탁드려요.
I just submitted it for approval, so please take a look.
everyday: 부탁드려요 is the polite 'I ask of you'
부장님 결재가 아직 안 나서 진행을 못 하고 있어요.
The manager's sign-off hasn't come through yet, so I can't proceed.
real situation: 아서 'because' chains the reason to the result
nuance: 결재 is the formal sign-off a superior puts on a document or expenditure before it can proceed, today usually through groupware (전자결재). It is Sino-Korean 決裁, literally 'decide-judge' — a person with authority decides and cuts a ruling. The make-or-break point for everyone, Koreans included, is the homophone pair 결재 (approval) vs 결제 (決濟, payment) — pronounced almost identically but meaning sign-off vs paying money; mixing the spelling is the single most common Korean office typo, so a learner who gets it right looks sharp. Directionally, 결재 flows up: a junior 결재를 올리다/받다, while the boss 결재를 하다/내주다. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you're the requester — you don't 'do' the approval, you 받다 (receive) it; only the approver does the 하다.

usage: to go to a client's place
에 marks the destination you visit
와 'with', 미팅 is everyday office English
에 marks the party you reach out to
examples: 거래처에서 전화 왔어요.
There's a call from the client.
simple: 에서 marks the source of the call
그 거래처는 결제가 항상 늦어요.
That client always pays late.
everyday: note 결제 'payment' here, not 결재
새 거래처를 뚫어서 이번 분기 매출이 올랐어요.
We landed a new account, so revenue rose this quarter.
real situation: 뚫다 'break through' = win a new client, slangy and proud
nuance: 거래처 means a company you do business with — depending on context a client, a vendor, or a supplier. It is built from native + Sino parts: 거래 (去來, 'go-come' = transactions/dealings) + 처 (處, 'place'), literally 'the place transactions happen', i.e. your business counterparty. The synonym line to hold: 거래처 is the B2B partner firm, 고객 (顧客) is a 'customer/client' broadly (can be an individual or a company), and 손님 is a face-to-face 'guest/customer' who walks in. A salesperson proudly says 거래처를 뚫다 (literally 'break through a client') to mean they won a new account. The English-speaker pitfall is calling an individual contact your 거래처 — the word denotes the company/account, not the person; for the person you'd say 거래처 담당자 (the contact at the client). Also don't downgrade a business partner to 손님, which sounds like a retail walk-in.

usage: 오르다 intransitive 'rise', sales rise on their own
올리다 transitive 'raise', you actively raise it
목표 (目標) 'goal/target', a constant team phrase
examples: 이번 달 매출이 어때요?
How are this month's sales?
simple: 어때요 'how is it' asks for an assessment
코로나 때 매출이 반으로 떨어졌어요.
During COVID sales dropped by half.
everyday: 반으로 '(down) to half', 으로 marks the result
매출 목표를 못 채워서 팀 전체가 스트레스받고 있어요.
We couldn't hit the sales target, so the whole team is stressed.
real situation: 채우다 'fill/meet (a quota)' is the set verb with 목표
nuance: 매출 is top-line sales/revenue — the gross money coming in before any costs are subtracted. It is Sino-Korean 賣出, literally 'sell-out', i.e. what you sold out the door. The crucial business-vocabulary contrast is 매출 (revenue, total inflow) vs 이익/수익 (利益/收益, profit = what's left after costs): a company can have huge 매출 but tiny 이익. Its life-partners are the rise/fall pair 오르다/떨어지다 (intransitive) and 올리다/낮추다 (transitive), plus 매출 목표 and 매출을 채우다 (meet the sales quota). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) confusing 'sales/revenue' with 'profit' — keep 매출 ≠ 이익 firmly apart; and (2) describing a big figure with 많다 ('many') as in 매출이 많다 — for a high amount Koreans say 매출이 높다 ('high'), since 매출 is a measured level, not a count of items.

examples: 저는 마케팅 부서예요.
I'm in the marketing department.
simple: 예요 lets you state your placement without a verb
다음 달에 다른 부서로 옮겨요.
Next month I'm transferring to another department.
everyday: 로 marks the destination department
그건 우리 부서 일이 아니라서 저는 잘 몰라요.
That's not our department's job, so I don't really know.
real situation: 아니라서 'because it isn't', polite way to deflect
nuance: 부서 is the general word for an organizational unit inside a company — a department or division. It is Sino-Korean 部署, where 部 means 'section/division' (the same 部 in 부장 department head) and 署 'a post/office'. The structural distinction newcomers must internalize: a 부서 is the broad department, a 팀 (team) is usually a smaller working unit inside or alongside it, and 부 alone (영업부, 인사부) is the formal divisional name. Beware the look-alike trap 부서 (the department, a place/unit) vs 부장 (部長, the department HEAD, a person) — one letter apart but unit vs human. New hires hear 어느 부서예요? on loop during introductions, so keep it primed. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 부서 and 팀 as interchangeable the way English flips 'department/team'; in a Korean org chart they sit at different levels, and you transfer between them with 옮기다, not 바꾸다 ('swap/change an object').

Saying 부서를 바꾸다 for a transfer — 바꾸다 means swapping an object; moving yourself to another department is 부서를 옮기다

usage: 님 is obligatory when addressing or referring up
되다 'become', the standard 'get promoted to' verb
to report to the team lead
한테 'to (a person)', casual counterpart of 에게
examples: 저희 팀장님이세요.
This is my team lead.
simple: 이세요 adds the subject honorific 시 to introduce a superior
이번에 팀장으로 승진했어요.
I got promoted to team lead this time.
everyday: 으로 marks the rank you were promoted into
팀장님한테 먼저 보고하고 나서 진행할게요.
I'll report to the team lead first and then proceed.
real situation: 고 나서 'after doing', sequencing two actions
nuance: 팀장 is the team leader — in many Korean companies your most immediate boss, the person you report to daily. It is Sino-Korean 팀(team) + 長 ('head/chief'), the same 長 that ends every Korean rank title: 부장 (department head), 사장 (company president), 회장 (chairman). Two register rules are non-negotiable: (1) you almost always attach 님 — 팀장님 — when speaking to or about them, and (2) you can use the bare rank 팀장 as a respectful address by itself, but never 팀장씨, because 씨 is a peer-level marker that, attached to a superior's title, sounds rude. Knowing 팀장 anchors the whole ladder (팀장 → 부장 → 이사 → 대표). The English-speaker pitfall is importing the Western habit of first names or a flat 'you' for managers: dropping 님 or using 씨 with a boss is a real status error Koreans notice instantly.

usage: the single most-used email noun phrase
에 marks what you attach it onto
습니다 formal ending, standard in business mail
examples: 여기 첨부했어요.
I've attached it here.
simple: short status line in a chat or message
첨부 파일을 확인해 주세요.
Please check the attached file.
everyday: near-mandatory closing line of a work email
보고서를 메일에 첨부했으니 확인 후 회신 부탁드립니다.
I've attached the report to the email, so please reply after reviewing.
real situation: 후 'after', 회신 'a reply', stiff business register
nuance: 첨부 means attaching a file to a message, and 첨부 파일 (attached file) is one of the highest-frequency phrases in Korean work email. It is Sino-Korean 添附, literally 'add-attach', both characters meaning to append something extra. The distinction to keep is digital 첨부하다 (attach an email file) vs physical 붙이다 (stick/glue something to a surface) vs 부착하다 (affix a label/poster) — English says 'attach' for all three, but a file is only ever 첨부하다. Its fixed companion line 첨부 파일을 확인해 주세요 is basically email etiquette you can paste anywhere. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond reaching for 붙이다, is spacing: in careful business writing it is two words, 첨부 파일, not 첨부파일 (though the squished form is tolerated in casual chat). Also note 첨부 has no plain past on its own — you write 첨부했어요/첨부했습니다, never 첨부 했어요 with a gap.

usage: to go out for field work
나가다 'go out', you leave the office
to be out on field work
중이다 'in the middle of', shows in-progress status
a compact schedule note on a calendar
to have a lot of field work
많다 describes frequency of the duty
examples: 저 지금 외근이에요.
I'm out on field work right now.
simple: noun + 이에요 states your current status
김 대리님은 지금 외근 중이세요.
Mr. Kim is out in the field right now.
everyday: 중이세요 adds honorific 시 when covering for a senior
영업직이라 외근이 많아서 사무실에 거의 없어요.
I'm in sales, so I'm rarely in the office because of all the field work.
real situation: 이라 'being (a job)' gives the reason
nuance: 외근 means working outside the office — visiting clients, sites, or branches during the workday. It is Sino-Korean 外勤, literally 'outside-duty', and its exact mirror is 내근 (內勤, 'inside-duty' = desk/in-office work); the 勤 ('duty/labor') here is the same character in 출근 (going to work) and 야근 (night work). The synonym line learners must draw is 외근 vs 출장 (出張): 외근 is a same-day excursion you return from by evening, while 출장 is a longer trip, often overnight or to another city. Saying 외근 중이에요 is the neat, professional way to explain why a coworker isn't at their seat. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'out of the office' as one bucket: don't use 외근 for going home, taking leave, or a multi-day trip — it specifically means leaving the building on work business and coming back. Use the action verb 나가다 (외근 나가다), not 가다 alone, for heading out.

usage: the noun takes 하다 to become a verb
가능하다 (可能) 'be possible', a job-hunting keyword
주 N회 'N times a week', 재택 is the clipped form
examples: 오늘 재택이에요.
I'm working from home today.
simple: clipped 재택 + 이에요 in casual speech
저희 회사는 재택근무가 가능해요.
Our company allows working from home.
everyday: 가능해요 frames it as a permitted perk
재택근무하니까 출퇴근 시간이 없어서 너무 편해요.
Since I work from home, there's no commute, so it's really comfortable.
real situation: 니까 'because/since' gives the reason for the upside
nuance: 재택근무 is the formal term for working from home, very commonly clipped to just 재택 in speech (오늘 재택이에요). It is fully Sino-Korean 在宅勤務, parsing as 在 'be located' + 宅 'home/residence' + 근무 'duty/work' — literally 'home-located work duty'. It exploded into daily vocabulary after COVID, so 재택근무 가능해요? is now a normal thing to ask when job hunting. The synonym field: 재택근무 (at home specifically) sits inside the broader 원격근무 (遠隔, 'remote work' from anywhere), while 외근 (off-site duty) is its near-opposite — leaving to go OUT, not staying in. The English-speaker pitfall is inventing a descriptive phrase like 집에서 근무 or 집에서 일해요 as if it were the term: those describe the activity, but the fixed noun is 재택근무. Also keep it apart from 외근 — both involve not sitting at your assigned office desk, but 재택은 home, 외근 is the field.

usage: the noun takes 하다 for the verb
많다 describes how often it happens
맨날 is casual 'every day', exasperated tone
examples: 오늘도 야근이에요.
I'm working late again today.
simple: 도 'also/again' hints this is a pattern
야근하면 야근 수당 나와요?
If I work late, do I get overtime pay?
everyday: 나오다 'come out (be paid)' is the set verb for 수당
요즘 프로젝트 때문에 매일 야근해서 너무 피곤해요.
Lately I work late every day because of a project, so I'm exhausted.
real situation: 때문에 'because of (a noun)' pins the cause
nuance: 야근 specifically means staying at the office working late into the night — the iconic symbol of old-school Korean work culture. It is Sino-Korean 夜勤, literally 'night-duty', sharing the 勤 ('duty/labor') of 외근 and 출근. The contrast to nail: 야근 is overtime that runs LATE/at night, whereas 특근 (特勤, 'special duty') and 추가 근무 cover extra work generally, including daytime, weekends, or holidays — so weekend morning work is 특근, not 야근. Its cultural foil is the slang 칼퇴 ('knife-exit' = leaving on the dot at quitting time), the thing everyone dreams of instead. And the carrot is 야근 수당 (overtime pay), which is 나오다 (paid out), not 받다-only. The English-speaker pitfall is using 야근 as a blanket word for all 'overtime' — keep the time-of-day nuance — and saying 야근을 가다 ('go to overtime'); you don't go to it, you 야근을 하다.

usage: 휴가 (休暇) spells out the fuller formal term
examples: 내일 연차예요.
I'm off (on leave) tomorrow.
simple: noun + 예요 announces the day off
올해 연차가 아직 5일 남았어요.
I still have 5 days of leave left this year.
everyday: 남다 'remain' reports the leftover balance
다음 주 금요일에 연차 내고 여행 가려고요.
I'm going to take leave next Friday and go on a trip.
real situation: 려고요 '(I) intend to', stating a plan
nuance: 연차 is your annual paid-vacation entitlement, counted and consumed in days. It is Sino-Korean 年次, literally 'year-order/yearly' (short for 연차 휴가, 年次休暇 'annual leave'). The synonym boundary learners blur: 휴가 (休暇) is the broad umbrella 'leave/vacation' of any kind (including 병가 sick leave, 여름 휴가 summer vacation), while 연차 is the specific paid days you accrue per year — so 연차 is one type of 휴가. A vital partner word is 반차 (半次, 'half-day leave') for slipping out for just a morning or afternoon. The verbs are fixed: you 연차를 쓰다 (use) or 연차를 내다 (file/submit), and your balance 남다 (remains). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: treating 연차 and 휴가 as fully interchangeable (휴가 is broader), and reaching for 하다 — there is no 연차를 하다; the leave is something you 쓰다 or 내다, not 'do'.
